sources.headline: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip
sources.text: Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America.Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory".On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire.There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love."The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope.He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.Read more on the significance of the Pope's visit to Peru

sources.headline: Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
sources.text: Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already.The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman.In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality.“The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said.Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo, a major city in the north.Leo is the first Peruvian citizen to become pope.The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery.Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6.In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River.Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment.He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion.“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out ⁠to God and demands justice.”Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning.Leo is expected to return to Rome on Monday.

Pope Leo visits high Andes, testing recovery from lung cancer surgery

The pope, who had part of a lung removed a month ago, arrived in the ancient Inca capital which is 3,400 metres above sea level

Published: 1:29am, 16 Nov 2026

Pope Leo on Sunday faced his toughest physical test since undergoing lung cancer surgery, visiting high-altitude Cusco on the final full day of his South America tour.

The 71-year-old pontiff, who had part of a lung removed a month ago, arrived in the ancient Inca capital, more than 3,400 metres (11,000ft) above sea level – high enough to leave many a visitor breathless.

Children in brightly woven ponchos and embroidered skirts greeted the pope as he stepped off the plane for the latest stop on an intense 12-day trip through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

“To be honest, I thought it might be cancelled,” said Valentin Cruz Turpo, aged 29. “But I still had hope, because God is powerful and can do anything.”

Hundreds of thousands lined the streets of a city that for centuries before the Spanish conquest was the “navel of the world” – a hub of learning and discovery in art, science and culture.

The pope visited a vast stone fortress that crowns a hill above Cusco, where troupes of musicians and ritual dancers from across the mountains gathered for a prayer service.

“The beauty of this place that welcomes us this morning is undeniable,” said the pontiff. “Saqsaywaman rises toward the Andean sky like a stone altar, where the ancients climbed in search of the divine.”

Under light drizzle, the faithful cheered him on.

“There has come to be a meeting point between the Catholic faith and the Andean beliefs that we have,” said engineer Adriano Fuyo Mora, 35, who described himself as “Catholic, Christian, and above all as an Andean, drawing on the traditions of my parents and ancestors”.

Participants dressed in traditional Andean attire attend a meeting between Pope Leo and representatives of popular devotion at the Saqsaywaman archaeological park in Cusco, Peru on Sunday. Photo: AFP

Later on Sunday he will be travelling to the Peruvian Amazon as part of a demanding day that will be closely watched for signs that his recovery remains on track.

The US-born pope spent nearly two decades as a missionary in Peru before becoming head of the Catholic Church.

His homecoming has included emotional reunions in Chiclayo, where he served as bishop, and repeated references to the country he has described as his adopted homeland.

His recent surgery cast doubt on whether the trip could go ahead as planned.

But Leo kept the demanding itinerary, thanking Peruvians on Friday for their prayers and support, “in particular for my health”.

In South America, home to the world’s largest Catholic population, Leo has sought to reinvigorate a faith that is losing followers in parts of the region.

He has used the trip to defend the poor and marginalised, denounce violence and express concern over falling birth rates.

01:58
Filipino Catholics pray for Pope Leo’s recovery after lung cancer surgery

Later on Sunday the pope was scheduled to fly to Pucallpa, one of the largest cities in the Peruvian Amazon, to meet indigenous leaders and hear concerns about threats facing rainforest communities.

Located on the Ucayali River, Pucallpa is at the heart of a region that has become one of Peru’s deforestation hotspots.

According to government figures, Peru lost 3.2 million hectares of forest between 2001 and 2024 – an area the size of Belgium.

Indigenous leader Fernando Carteiro said local communities hoped the pope would draw attention to their struggle.

“The message he can give is not only for Peru, it will be for the whole world,” he told Agence France-Presse, adding that communities would welcome a pope willing to “speak on our side”.

The Pope was expected to watch a traditional Shipibo-Konibo dance before delivering remarks expected to focus on drug trafficking, illegal logging and pollution in the Amazon.

He will also take part in a ceremony involving a shihuahuaco tree, an Amazon species prized by loggers but capable of living for more than 1,000 years, before celebrating a mass and returning to Lima.

Just a year and a half into his papacy and less than a month after surgeons removed a lobe of his right lung, Pope Leo XIV, the first pontiff born in the United States, touched down in his homeland on Wednesday.Yet instead of setting foot on American soil, he arrived in Peru, where he spent two decades as a missionary, priest and bishop and became a citizen in 2015.“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said, speaking on Wednesday evening to Peru’s president, civic leaders and diplomats at the Gran Teatro Nacional, a theater and concert hall in the country’s capital, Lima. One of his biggest applause lines was when he referred to Peru as “my homeland.”Having turned out record crowds at Masses in Argentina, the pope flew from Buenos Aires to Lima on Wednesday afternoon, reaching the final country of his 12-day tour of South America. The pope emerged at the top of the stairs next to a sign on the side of his plane that read “Pontifex Maximus,” and was greeted by Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, and a chorus of singing children on a red carpet at the Callao Air Base near Lima.As his motorcade made its way through city streets under gray skies, about 3 million people lined the roads, according to local authorities, holding up cellphones as they waited for a glimpse of the pontiff.His choice to visit Peru so soon after becoming pope — while deferring a visit to the country of his birth — underscored the deep emotional ties he feels to the place that formed him as a priest.Thank you for your patience while we verify access. sources.headline: Pope declares Peru his "homeland" in final leg of South America trip
sources.text:
Updated on: November 12, 2026 / 2:26 PM EST
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
Pope Leo XIV declared Peru his "homeland" on Wednesday as he arrived in Lima at the start of his historic visit, returning to the place that taught him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party erupted to welcome the beloved "Padre Robert" home.Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his charter plane, smiling broadly at nearly every turn of his first moments on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated that some 3 million people lined Leo's miles-long motorcade route into town, waving Peruvian and Holy See flags.Some in the roaring crowds broke through the tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace, where Leo met privately with Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori. During the formal welcome ceremony in the palace courtyard, he sang the Peruvian national anthem alongside Fujimori and a children's choir.
Pope Leo waves to the faithful from the popemobile on his way to Peru's government palace in Lima on Nov. 11, 2026.
Miguel Marruffo /AFP via Getty Images
In his first remarks to Fujimori and government officials, the Chicago-born Leo said the Peruvian citizenship he acquired in 2015 cemented a bond that began long before, crediting Peruvians with having formed him as a pastor by sharing their lives, joys and struggles with him."Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said."That is why I can tell you, with deep gratitude, that I am also returning to my homeland," he said to applause.Popemania descends on Peru, where Leo lived and served for decadesThe visit to Peru marked the final leg of Leo's three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that Leo, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. He has said it was here that he learned "what it means to be a shepherd." As a dual citizen of the U.S. and Peru, he's the first pope from each country.
"We love him so much because he's worked here, he knows our sufferings, he knows it all," said 85-year-old Evelina Cruz, who held a pope plush doll made by her niece as she waited for Leo to arrive.
Pope Leo XIV and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori at a welcome ceremony as part of the pope's official visit to Peru at the Presidential Palace on Nov. 11, 2026, in Lima, Peru.
Mariana Bazo / Getty Images
In preparation for the pope's visit, a huge 46-foot statue of the pontiff was unveiled in the port of El Callao. Baristas in Lima, the capital, were offering cappuccinos decorated with the image of the pope."My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy," said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo's secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast.
Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of "Lived Religion in Latin America," said the trip was a "return to his origins, without any doubt.""Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born," he said.With hands raised and voices lifted in song, hundreds awaited the pope's arrival in Lima in front of the presidential palace. "Long live Christ!" the crowd sang, following a Catholic choir on the stage.Popemania also hit Chiclayo, where Leo arrives on Friday. Leo is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on T-shirts, baseball hats and even bobblehead dolls.Over the coming days, Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including at the nearby sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, a city that is a hub of Afro-Peruvian culture, and where the pope often visited to pray to the saint of his devotion.Since Leo knows his adopted country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he'll deliver from the square in front of Lima's cathedral Thursday "on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people."Pope to honor Peru's Indigenous peoples in the AmazonThe pope will honor Peru's Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, in Peru's Amazon, to celebrate Mass. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Peru's Indigenous peoples.
"The Amazon is a place where critical issues affecting development — such as the environmental crisis, the exclusion of Indigenous peoples, various forms of violence, and extreme poverty — all intersect," said Pérez.Leo will also meet with popular groups of faithful and representatives of local traditions in Cusco — the capital of the Inca Empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and an important cultural destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu.The pope will celebrate Mass in Cusco's main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era.Pope arrives in Peru about one month after undergoing lung cancer surgeryThe pope's arrival in Peru comes about one month after he underwent surgery in Italy to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, during which surgeons confirmed he had lung cancer. The Vatican announced at the time that the 71-year-old had been diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, and that the surgery had been successful. Just two weeks after he underwent the surgery, doctors cleared him to make the South American trip, which started in Uruguay and took him to Argentina.During an address in Uruguay last weekend, the pope used his own experience with cancer to push for access to universal healthcare.
"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness, and I received care for which I am grateful," the pope said. " … Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society."At the start of his trip, the pope also confirmed that he voted by mail in the U.S. midterm elections in Chicago, the first sitting pontiff to vote in a U.S. election.
